questions.q: Which coenzyme form of vitamin B1 (thiamine) is required by pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase?
questions.explain: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is the active coenzyme form of vitamin B1 and acts as a carrier of activated aldehyde/hydroxyethyl groups in oxidative decarboxylations and transketolase reactions. PLP is derived from vitamin B6, FAD from B2, and THF from folate.

open.q: Which active coenzyme derivative of vitamin B1 is required for oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids and transketolase activity?

questions.q: A patient with chronic alcohol use disorder presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion. Administration of which vitamin prior to glucose infusion helps prevent precipitation of acute encephalopathy?
questions.explain: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and beriberi due to impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase activity. Giving glucose without thiamine increases metabolic demand on thiamine-dependent enzymes and can worsen acute Wernicke encephalopathy.

open.q: Deficiency of which vitamin causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and beriberi?

questions.q: Which two redox coenzymes are synthesized from riboflavin (vitamin B2)?
questions.explain: Riboflavin forms flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), which act as electron carriers in redox reactions such as succinate dehydrogenase and acyl-CoA dehydrogenase. NAD+ and NADP+ are derived from niacin (vitamin B3).

open.q: Which two coenzymes are derived from vitamin B2 (riboflavin)?
accept: flavin mononucleotide and flavin adenine dinucleotide

questions.q: Which clinical signs are classically associated with riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency?
options: Cheilosis, angular stomatitis, and magenta tongue (glossitis)
Night blindness, xerophthalmia, and Bitot spots
Microcytic hypochromic anemia and palmar hyperkeratosis
questions.explain: Riboflavin deficiency (ariboflavinosis) typically causes mucocutaneous lesions including cheilosis (fissuring at lip corners), angular stomatitis, glossitis, and corneal vascularization. Night blindness and xerophthalmia reflect vitamin A deficiency.

open.q: Which mucocutaneous signs such as cheilosis and angular stomatitis are characteristic of riboflavin deficiency?
accept: angular cheilitis, stomatitis, and magenta tongue

questions.q: Which essential amino acid serves as an endogenous metabolic precursor for niacin (NAD+/NADP+) synthesis in humans?
questions.explain: Humans can synthesize small amounts of niacin from tryptophan via the kynurenine pathway, requiring vitamin B6 (PLP) as a cofactor. Dietary deficiency of both niacin and tryptophan (such as in maize-predominant diets) predisposes to pellagra.

open.q: Which amino acid can be converted endogenously into niacin in human tissues?

questions.q: Which classic triad of clinical features characterizes pellagra due to niacin deficiency?
questions.explain: Pellagra is classically summarized by the three Ds: photosensitive dermatitis (especially on sun-exposed skin), diarrhea, and dementia (with death if untreated). High-dose niacin is also used clinically to lower LDL cholesterol and raise HDL.

open.q: What is the classic clinical triad of pellagra caused by niacin deficiency?
accept: the three Ds: dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia

questions.q: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) is a structural component of coenzyme A and which other acyl-carrying molecule?
questions.explain: Pantothenic acid provides the 4-phosphopantetheine moiety with a reactive sulfhydryl (-SH) group in both coenzyme A (CoA) and fatty acid synthase's acyl carrier protein (ACP). These thiol groups form high-energy thioester bonds with acyl groups.

open.q: Besides coenzyme A, which acyl-transporting protein incorporates pantothenic acid?

questions.q: Which coenzyme derived from vitamin B6 is essential for transamination, decarboxylation, and glycogen phosphorylase activity?
questions.explain: Pyridoxal 5-phosphate (PLP) forms Schiff base (aldimine) intermediates with amino acids during transaminations (aminotransferases), decarboxylations (such as neurotransmitter synthesis), and heme synthesis (ALA synthase). It also serves as a cofactor for glycogen phosphorylase.

open.q: Which vitamin B6 coenzyme acts in transamination and decarboxylation of amino acids?

questions.q: A patient taking isoniazid for pulmonary tuberculosis develops peripheral neuropathy and sideroblastic anemia. Co-administration of which vitamin prevents these adverse effects?
questions.explain: Isoniazid induces pyridoxine deficiency by increasing excretion or forming hydrazones with PLP, impairing GABA synthesis (causing peripheral neuropathy) and ALA synthase activity (impairing heme synthesis and causing sideroblastic anemia). Prophylactic pyridoxine prevents this.

open.q: Which vitamin is co-administered with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy and sideroblastic anemia?

questions.q: Which metabolic reaction type is catalyzed by biotin-dependent enzymes such as pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase?
questions.explain: Biotin acts as a mobile carrier of activated carbon dioxide (carboxybiotin) in ATP-dependent carboxylation reactions, including pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and propionyl-CoA carboxylase. Raw egg white protein avidin binds biotin tightly and can cause deficiency.

open.q: Which type of biochemical reaction do biotin-dependent enzymes like pyruvate carboxylase catalyze?

questions.q: Which coenzyme form of folic acid is generated by dihydrofolate reductase and serves as a carrier of one-carbon units?
questions.explain: Folate is reduced via dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate (THF) by dihydrofolate reductase, then carries one-carbon units (methyl, methylene, methenyl, formyl) needed for purine and thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase.

open.q: Which active reduced form of folate carries one-carbon groups in nucleotide biosynthesis?

questions.q: A pregnant patient presents with megaloblastic anemia and a normal serum vitamin B12 level. Periconceptional supplementation with which vitamin reduces the risk of fetal neural tube defects such as spina bifida?
questions.explain: Folate deficiency impairs thymidylate and purine synthesis needed for DNA replication, causing megaloblastic anemia and elevating homocysteine without neurologic signs. Adequate periconceptional folic acid markedly lowers neural tube defect risk.

open.q: Periconceptional supplementation with which vitamin prevents neural tube defects and treats folate-deficiency megaloblastic anemia?

questions.q: Which two enzymatic reactions in humans require vitamin B12 (cobalamin) coenzymes?
questions.explain: Methylcobalamin is a cofactor for methionine synthase (converting homocysteine to methionine and regenerating THF), while 5-deoxyadenosylcobalamin is required by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (converting L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA). Deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neurologic degeneration.

open.q: Name the two human enzymes that require vitamin B12 coenzymes as cofactors.

questions.q: Why does vitamin B12 deficiency lead to functional folate trapping (methyl trap) in the cell?
options: 5-methyl-THF cannot be demethylated to THF via homocysteine without methylcobalamin
Dihydrofolate reductase is permanently inactivated by excess vitamin B12
Folate is converted into insoluble uric acid in the kidney
Intrinsic factor degrades folate inside gastric parietal cells
questions.explain: Without methylcobalamin for methionine synthase, one-carbon units become trapped as 5-methyl-THF, limiting regeneration of free THF needed for purine and dTMP synthesis. This explains why folate supplements can partially correct B12 megaloblastic anemia without preventing neurologic damage.

open.q: How does vitamin B12 deficiency cause folate to become trapped in the 5-methyl-THF form?
accept: lack of methylcobalamin blocks methionine synthase demethylation of 5-methyl-THF
impaired methionine synthase activity prevents conversion of 5-methyl-THF to THF

questions.q: Which glycoprotein secreted by gastric parietal cells is required for intestinal absorption of vitamin B12?
questions.explain: Gastric parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which binds cobalamin in the duodenum and enables uptake via cubilin receptors in the terminal ileum. Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells or intrinsic factor causes pernicious anemia.

open.q: Which gastric parietal cell factor is necessary for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum?

questions.q: How does vitamin C (ascorbic acid) enhance non-heme dietary iron absorption in the gastrointestinal tract?
options: Reduces ferric iron (Fe3+) to the more soluble ferrous state (Fe2+)
Binds iron covalently to form an insoluble fecal complex
Increases gastric pH to precipitate ferric hydroxide
questions.explain: Ascorbic acid acts as a reducing agent in the gut lumen, keeping dietary non-heme iron in the reduced ferrous (Fe2+) state that is more soluble and readily absorbed across enterocytes. It also serves as a reducing cofactor for hydroxylases and dopamine beta-hydroxylase.

open.q: How does ascorbic acid promote intestinal absorption of non-heme iron?
accept: converts ferric iron to ferrous iron
maintains iron in the ferrous state

questions.q: Which visual pigment derivative of vitamin A combines with opsin in rod photoreceptors to mediate vision in dim light?
questions.explain: 11-cis-retinal binds opsin to form rhodopsin in rod cells; absorption of a photon isomerizes 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, triggering a phototransduction cascade. Retinoic acid regulates gene transcription via nuclear receptors but does not form the visual chromophore.

open.q: Which isomer of retinal combines with opsin to form rhodopsin for dim-light vision?

questions.q: Which form of vitamin A functions primarily in regulating gene expression and epithelial cell differentiation rather than vision?
questions.explain: Retinoic acid binds retinoic acid receptors (RAR) and retinoid X receptors (RXR) to regulate transcription and epithelial differentiation, preventing squamous metaplasia. It cannot be reduced back to retinal or retinol.

open.q: Which retinoid acts mainly through nuclear receptors to regulate gene transcription and epithelial differentiation?

questions.q: A child with severe malnutrition presents with dry conjunctiva, Bitot spots, night blindness, and recurrent respiratory infections. Deficiency of which vitamin underlies these findings?
questions.explain: Vitamin A deficiency causes xerophthalmia (night blindness, conjunctival and corneal xerosis, Bitot spots, keratomalacia) and impairs mucosal epithelial barriers and immune function. Excess vitamin A is teratogenic and hepatotoxic.

open.q: Deficiency of which vitamin causes night blindness, Bitot spots, and xerophthalmia?

questions.q: Which active hormonal form of vitamin D increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and acts with parathyroid hormone on bone?
questions.explain: Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol) is the active hormone synthesized via 25-hydroxylation in the liver and 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the kidney. It increases intestinal calcium-binding protein (calbindin) synthesis and raises serum calcium and phosphate.

open.q: What is the biologically most active hormonal form of vitamin D?

questions.q: In which organ does 25-hydroxylase convert cholecalciferol into 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol), the main circulating storage form?
questions.explain: The liver converts vitamin D3 or D2 into 25-hydroxyvitamin D via 25-hydroxylase, providing the major circulating form measured to assess vitamin D status. Subsequent 1-alpha-hydroxylation occurs mainly in renal proximal tubules.

open.q: Which organ performs the 25-hydroxylation step that forms calcidiol (25-hydroxyvitamin D)?

questions.q: What bone disorder develops in children due to defective mineralization of growing osteoid and epiphyseal cartilage from vitamin D deficiency?
questions.explain: In children prior to epiphyseal fusion, vitamin D deficiency impairs bone and growth-plate mineralization, causing rickets (bowing of weight-bearing bones, rachitic rosary, craniotabes). In adults after epiphyseal closure, impaired osteoid mineralization causes osteomalacia.

open.q: Which childhood bone mineralization disorder is classically caused by vitamin D deficiency?

questions.q: What is the primary biochemical role of vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) in cell membranes?
options: Chain-breaking lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects polyunsaturated fatty acids from peroxidation
Coenzyme for carboxylation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X
Visual chromophore required for rod cell rhodopsin regeneration
Carrier of activated one-carbon units in purine synthesis
questions.explain: Alpha-tocopherol is a lipid-soluble antioxidant embedded in membranes that donates a hydrogen atom to lipid peroxyl radicals, terminating lipid peroxidation chains. It works alongside selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase.

open.q: How does vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) protect cell membranes from oxidative damage?
accept: acts as a chain-breaking antioxidant in membranes

questions.q: Which clinical manifestations can occur with severe vitamin E deficiency?
options: Spinocerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, and hemolytic anemia
Bilateral parotid enlargement and dental fluorosis
questions.explain: Vitamin E deficiency increases erythrocyte fragility (hemolytic anemia, especially in premature infants) and causes neurologic dysfunction including posterior column and spinocerebellar degeneration (ataxia, areflexia). It is often associated with fat malabsorption or abetalipoproteinemia.

open.q: Name one neurological or hematologic feature of vitamin E deficiency.

questions.q: Which post-translational modification of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X requires vitamin K as a cofactor?
options: Gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues to form gamma-carboxyglutamate (Gla)
Phosphorylation of serine residues by ATP
Hydroxylation of proline residues in collagen
questions.explain: Vitamin K is an essential cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which converts specific glutamate (Glu) residues into gamma-carboxyglutamate (Gla) on clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S. Gla residues chelate calcium ions needed for phospholipid membrane binding.

open.q: Which modification of glutamate residues on clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X requires vitamin K?

questions.q: How does warfarin exert its anticoagulant effect in relation to the vitamin K cycle?
options: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing regeneration of reduced active vitamin K
Directly activates factor Xa and thrombin in plasma
Chelates dietary calcium in the intestinal lumen
questions.explain: During gamma-carboxylation, reduced vitamin K (hydroquinone) is oxidized to vitamin K epoxide, which must be reduced back by vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1). Warfarin inhibits VKORC1, depleting active reduced vitamin K and reducing functional Gla-modified clotting factors.

open.q: Which enzyme in the vitamin K cycle is inhibited by warfarin?

questions.q: A 4-day-old exclusively breastfed neonate who did not receive a birth injection presents with generalized bleeding, prolonged prothrombin time (PT), and normal platelet count. Which vitamin deficiency explains hemorrhagic disease of the newborn?
questions.explain: Newborns have low transplacental vitamin K stores, sterile guts with minimal menaquinone-producing bacteria initially, and low vitamin K content in breast milk. Vitamin K deficiency prolongs PT and aPTT and causes bleeding prevented by intramuscular vitamin K at birth.

open.q: Deficiency of which vitamin causes hemorrhagic disease of the newborn with a prolonged prothrombin time?

questions.q: Which coenzyme is derived from nicotinamide (niacin) and typically carries hydride ions (two electrons and one proton) in dehydrogenase reactions?
questions.explain: NAD+ and NADP+ accept a hydride ion (:H-) onto the nicotinamide ring to become NADH or NADPH, releasing one proton into solution. NAD+ is generally linked with catabolic oxidation, whereas NADPH provides reducing power for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense.

open.q: Which niacin-derived coenzyme accepts a hydride ion in oxidation-reduction reactions to form NADH?

questions.q: In which metabolic pathway is NADPH primarily generated for fatty acid synthesis, cholesterol synthesis, and glutathione reduction?
questions.explain: The oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway (via glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase) is a major source of cytosolic NADPH. NADPH supplies reducing equivalents for reductive biosynthesis and maintains reduced glutathione via glutathione reductase.

open.q: Which metabolic pathway is a major source of cytosolic NADPH for biosynthesis and glutathione reduction?

questions.q: Which coenzyme carries acyl groups via a reactive terminal sulfhydryl (-SH) group to form thioesters such as acetyl-CoA?
questions.explain: Coenzyme A (CoA-SH) contains a terminal thiol group that forms high-energy thioester bonds with carboxylic acids, activating acyl groups such as acetyl-CoA, succinyl-CoA, and fatty acyl-CoA. Thioesters have a higher group-transfer potential than ordinary oxygen esters.

open.q: Which coenzyme forms high-energy thioester bonds with acyl groups such as acetyl and succinyl groups?
